subject: Business Models
title: Negative Pricing
description: A micro-lesson that makes Negative Pricing usable.

hook.text: Google pays Apple $20 billion per year to be the default search engine on iPhones. Google pays you to use it.

buildup.text: Negative pricing means the company pays the customer (or their gatekeeper) to use the product.

discovery.text: When the user's attention is the product, companies compete by paying distributors and customers for access.

twist.text: Credit card companies pay users via cashback. The merchants pay the fees. Users get paid to spend money.

climax.text: Negative pricing flips economics upside down. When data and attention are valuable, access is worth paying for.

punchline.text: $20B to be the default. When attention is the product, the user gets paid.

quiz.question: Why does Google pay Apple $20 billion per year?
options: To be the default search engine on iPhones

details.summary: Negative pricing pays customers to use a product, subsidized by revenue from a third party or future monetization. Cashback apps, paid survey platforms, and sign-up bonuses all use negative pricing to acquire users whose attention or data generates value elsewhere.
details.whyItMatters: Negative pricing inverts the traditional customer-pays model. It reveals that in attention and data economies, the user is the product. Understanding it helps decode why companies pay you to use their services.
takeaways: Companies pay users to acquire attention, data, or network effects
Revenue from advertisers or data buyers subsidizes the user payments
Cashback apps and sign-up bonuses are common negative pricing examples

faq.question: How can paying customers be a profitable business model?
faq.answer: The payments are subsidized by third-party revenue. Cashback apps earn affiliate commissions exceeding what they pay users. Banks offer sign-up bonuses because lifetime customer revenue far exceeds the bonus. The user payment is a customer acquisition cost.

faq.question: What are the risks of negative pricing models?
faq.answer: Attracting deal-seekers who leave when subsidies end, unsustainable unit economics if third-party revenue does not materialize, regulatory scrutiny over data practices, and the difficulty of transitioning users to positive pricing after conditioning them to be paid.
